title: Jensen Huang: AI expanded compute a millionfold in a decade, not the hundredfold Moore's Law predicted
dek: Jensen Huang explains how pre-packaged software locked compute advances to Moore's Law's pace, while CUDA enabled simultaneous redesign of algorithms, precision, and chips—pushing compute roughly a millionfold over the past decade.
why: Rare technical interview where Jensen Huang systematically explains GPU design principles with no marketing speak and high information density—essential for understanding compute at first principles.
who: Engineers seeking to understand GPU and compute scaling fundamentals, plus investors evaluating whether compute investment narratives rest on solid technical ground.
skip: The opening ~2 minutes of warm-up Q&A (favorite programming language, games, etc.) can be skipped without affecting the technical content that follows.

points.h: Graphics rendering is becoming educated guessing
points.body: Huang explains that computer graphics now renders only one pixel truly, then infers the other fifteen, with colors temporally stable and matching real render results. This allows higher resolution and greater complexity rendering with better results than full rendering. He emphasizes AI isn't approximation but genuinely extends the limits of what physics and nearly every field can reach.

points.h: Graphics and compute cards split from one path; now they're merging back
points.body: Huang describes how GPUs originally forked into two branches: graphics-focused with 32-bit float dominance and deliberately slow double precision, and science computing with double precision pushed to extremes. The second fork came when AI's importance in datacenters overwhelmed everything else, adding tensor cores relentlessly—then moving them back into GeForce, letting graphics itself become AI-driven. His framing: GeForce brought CUDA to the world, CUDA made AI possible, and AI revolutionized GeForce in return.

points.h: Pre-packaged software locked compute into Moore's Law
points.body: When software was pre-compiled and stamped onto retail CD-ROMs, advances in CPU architecture—pipelining, superscalar execution, out-of-order execution—couldn't free software from the speed set at packaging time. This was Moore's Law's real constraint. The breakthrough was accelerated computing: software needn't change, but algorithm and chip could redesign together under CUDA—freeing software from the box, letting architecture, algorithm, and chip optimize as one.

points.h: Each precision step down yields fourfold compute gains
points.body: AI is fundamentally statistical: 1.1 + 1.3 ≈ 2 without high precision, so approximation suffices. Each drop from FP32 to FP16 to FP8 quadruples available compute or quarters energy cost. Computing architecture also shifts from vector operations to tensor cores, executing 32, 64, or even 128 instructions simultaneously, letting chip architecture truly match algorithm structure.

points.h: A millionfold decade, not Moore's Law's hundredfold
points.body: Huang attributes recent compute gains to multiple dimensions shifting together: single-chip parallelism, multiple chips, multiple nodes, multiple racks, plus full-stack optimization across algorithm, precision, and parallelization—stacking to roughly a millionfold scale increase over a decade versus ~hundredfold under old Moore's Law (hundredfold per decade). Notably, neural network architectures themselves are constantly reinvented—they're software, fundamentally plastic—with Transformer concepts evolving new structures.

points.h: Scale up first, then scale out
points.body: Huang distinguishes scale up (vertical scaling)—making one machine faster with almost no software change, but extremely difficult, limited by semiconductor physics and memory bandwidth—from scale out (horizontal scaling), breaking algorithms into distributed chunks like Hadoop/MapReduce. NVIDIA's NVLink lets many GPUs be programmed as one giant GPU, achieving the 'vertical scaling' semiconductor physics alone cannot, then layering horizontal scaling across multiple racks.

points.h: Amdahl's Law explains why CPUs remain absolutely essential
points.body: If only 10% of a task must execute sequentially, even infinite acceleration of the other 90% bottlenecks at that 10%; if you only accelerate the parallel part to equal the sequential part's time, total speedup is only 5x not 10x. Single-thread speed must be pushed to the limit in parallel machines—which is why NVIDIA builds CPUs itself chasing extreme single-thread performance, leaving parallel parts to CUDA.

points.h: 5G basebands on CUDA make wireless a robotics network
points.body: An unexpected CUDA use case Huang highlights: 5G radio baseband signal processing no longer uses custom silicon but runs directly on CUDA. Radio becomes software-defined, stacking or swapping AI layers—deep learning for baseband processing, AI for massive MIMO and multi-radio traffic scheduling. He argues wireless becomes fundamentally a robotics network, adding reinforcement learning lets algorithms become more adaptive and autonomous, potentially saving power and spectrum efficiency.

points.h: AI makes transmission a compute-for-bandwidth exchange
points.body: Huang describes a concrete case: after encoding and transmitting initial video call frames, later frames needn't encode frame-by-frame—neural networks regenerate matching facial movements from audio, as the other person is already 'known.' Adding human priors, generation directly replaces network bandwidth consumption; Huang cites 5G/6G bandwidth potentially dropping ~1000x—fundamentally using neural compute to replace transmission bandwidth.
